Rescorla-Wagner (1972) error-driven associative model

Source: R/model-rescorla_wagner.R
rescorla_wagner.Rd

On each trial, the words present are cues and the objects outcomes. Each outcome's prediction is the summed association of the present cues, and its prediction error (lambda - prediction if it is present, 0 - prediction if absent) changes every present cue's association with it by alpha * beta * lambda times the error. Cues therefore compete to predict an outcome (e.g. blocking: a word paired with an object that another word already predicts learns little about it). All associations then decay by C.

Usage

rescorla_wagner(
  C,
  alpha,
  beta,
  lambda,
  outcomes = c("present", "all"),
  cues = c("words", "objects"),
  phi = NULL
)

Arguments

C

Decay

alpha

Salience (fix at 1 unless manipulated)

beta

Learning rate – a proportion of lambda

lambda

Maximum associative value that a CS can achieve - should be larger than learning rate

outcomes

"present" (the default) updates only the objects present on a trial; "all" also updates absent objects toward 0.

cues

"words" (the default): words predict objects. "objects": objects predict words.

phi

Optional softmax inverse temperature for the choice rule. NULL (the default) uses Luce choice.

Value

An object of class xslMod

Details

The defaults (outcomes = "present", cues = "words", Luce choice) are the model as originally applied to cross-situational learning, which learns only about the objects present on a trial. In designs where every pair recurs, it then stays close to counting co-occurrences.

Options

  • outcomes = "all" follows Rescorla & Wagner (1972) in treating every possible outcome as present (target lambda) or absent (target 0) on every trial, so a word's associations with objects that are absent when it is heard weaken. This is discriminative learning (Ramscar et al., 2010; Baayen et al., 2011). Associations can then become negative, which Luce choice treats as 0; phi gives a choice rule defined for them.

  • cues = "objects" reverses the direction of prediction: objects are cues and words outcomes, as in Ramscar et al.'s (2010) feature-label ordering account. The matrix keeps words as rows (m[w, o] is object o's association with word w), and test choices are still made among a word's row. Cues now compete to predict words rather than objects, so the two directions learn different associations.

  • phi replaces Luce choice with a softmax choice rule with inverse temperature phi (see softmax_weights()), applied by xsl_run() and to the model's own perf.

Choice is invariant to the scale of the associations under Luce choice, and under softmax the scale trades off against phi, so lambda is not identifiable separately from beta (and phi): fix it (e.g. at 1) when fitting. Likewise alpha only enters as alpha * beta.

References

Baayen, R. H., Milin, P., Durdevic, D. F., Hendrix, P., & Marelli, M. (2011). An amorphous model for morphological processing in visual comprehension based on naive discriminative learning. Psychological Review, 118(3), 438-481.

Ramscar, M., Yarlett, D., Dye, M., Denny, K., & Thorpe, K. (2010). The effects of feature-label-order and their implications for symbolic learning. Cognitive Science, 34(6), 909-957.

Rescorla, R. A., & Wagner, A. R. (1972). A theory of Pavlovian conditioning: Variations in the effectiveness of reinforcement and nonreinforcement. In A. H. Black & W. F. Prokasy (Eds.), Classical conditioning II (pp. 64-99). Appleton-Century-Crofts.

Examples

mod <- rescorla_wagner(C = 1, alpha = 1, beta = 0.1, lambda = 3)
xsl_run(mod, get_example_ambiguous_condition())
#> $fits
#> $fits[[1]]
#> $fits[[1]]$sims
#> NULL
#> 
#> $fits[[1]]$responses
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]  0.5  0.5  0.5  0.5
#> 
#> $fits[[1]]$perf
#>   1   2   3   4 
#> 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 
#> 
#> $fits[[1]]$matrix
#>     1   2   3   4
#> 1 0.9 0.9 0.0 0.0
#> 2 0.9 0.9 0.0 0.0
#> 3 0.0 0.0 0.9 0.9
#> 4 0.0 0.0 0.9 0.9
#> 
#> $fits[[1]]$sse
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $fits[[1]]$data
#> xslData object with label "example condition" and condition "ambiguous"
#>   training trials: 2
#>       test trials: 0
#>             words: 4
#>           objects: 4
#>        accuracies: 4
#> 
#> 
#> 
#> $sse
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $unweighted_sse
#> [1] 0
#> 
# discriminative learning, with a softmax choice rule
mod <- rescorla_wagner(C = .98, alpha = 1, beta = .3, lambda = 1, outcomes = "all", phi = 5)
xsl_run(mod, get_example_ambiguous_condition())
